MECSR Directory 2027: session record

What happened

The session ran from 10 to 16 Oct 2026. The detailed history before 13 Oct survives only as a summary, so earlier sessions appear here as context.

DateWorkWhat came out of it
Aug–Sep 2026Earlier sessionsBrilliant Directories kit (import CSVs, admin guide, first verification tracker), the September verification playbook, the QR-slug workbook (4 Sep), the membership snapshot (4 Sep) and the scheduled tasks. Context only: those sessions are not part of this history.
10 Oct 2026Sample book v12 and the live flat planRebuilt the book to 384 pages (24 signatures of 16) from v10, with every two-page item opening on a left-hand page. Updated the content tracker from the RCM sponsor matrix of 8 Oct, the v12 pagination and the intel reports (sheets 10–13). Built the dossier and the GitHub flat-plan page that reads the workbook live.
10 Oct 2026Research and the design canvasTwo research agents ran 166 web searches: accessibility and English/Arabic standards, and a benchmark of the best digital directories. Their briefs shaped three design directions, built as six artboards on the design canvas.
12 Oct 2026QR codes out: sample book v13Brilliant Directories builds a listing's web address from its name, so renaming a listing breaks any printed code. v13 removes every QR code and rewrites pages 5, 78 and 381 to point readers to directory.mecsr.org. Updated the GitHub repository through the browser.
13 Oct 2026Photography and the seal: sample book v14Retail Congress MENA 2026 photographs on the awards page (66), the house ads (67–69), each sponsor's imagery page (21–31) and as stand-ins on the Expert Views, leadership pages and title-partner page. The MECSR Verified seal on 341 listing cards and the 7 Must-Visit pages. Seal added to the canvas. README and tracker committed (863118b).
13 Oct 2026Landlord verification campaignFrom Ian's note of 12 Oct: a plan and timeline (Claude Doc), ten eSputnik email templates with a preview page, and a campaign workbook. Finding: 654 of the 666 listings the export calls "Verified (2026)" share one bulk edit (26 Jun 2026, 09:51:06), so none is landlord-confirmed yet.
14 Oct 2026Canvas edit and new daily intel taskThe Field Guide phone artboard was adjusted in the design editor (scroll area height). A new scheduled task, MECSR Intel daily, started; two older intel tasks were switched off.
15 Oct 2026This recordFive HTML files: this summary, the PDF directory, the mobile and web apps, the sourcing and verification plan, and the memory handoff for another Claude account.
16 Oct 2026Openable everywhereIn the chat preview the file tabs gave a 404, because the other four files are not beside the one being previewed. Added an all-in-one file whose tabs work anywhere, published the record as a private page on claude.ai, and saved it into the Directory folder with offline copies of the campaign doc (PDF) and the canvas source.

Artifacts and online links

Artifacts are private to Orient's account until shared. To give a colleague access, open the artifact on claude.ai and press Share; a different Claude account cannot open these links otherwise. Anyone the links cannot reach gets the files instead: the campaign doc as a PDF and the canvas source are in Offline copies, and the dossier is the file MECSR_2027_Directory_Dossier.html.

Local files and folders

The working files sit in the MECSR team's OneDrive folder Directory 2026 and on the Retail Congress photo drive. This public edition names the files but leaves out the folders on staff computers.

File 01 of 04 · PDF directory

The PDF directory: sample book v14

The 384-page print and reading editions, how they were built from v10 to v14, the full page plan and what must be fixed before print.

What the book is

The MECSR Directory 2027 is a 384-page annual: sponsor showcases, expert views, country profiles, about 1,377 shopping-centre records in 31 countries, retail brands, service providers and member listings. The current sample is v14 of 13 Oct 2026.

384pages = 24 printer signatures of 16
91plan items, every page claimed once
40commercial pages (10.4%)
298pages generated from the master dataset
1 Jul 2027press date in the tracker
6 May 2027listing data freeze (press − 8 weeks)

Page 1 is a right-hand page, so every two-page item must start on an even page to print as a true spread. A page added anywhere is a page taken from somewhere else, or a whole new signature of 16.

Versions

Each build is two files: MECSR_Directory_2027_Sample_Book_v<N>.pdf in print order (page 1 is the front cover, the printer's file) and …_v<N>_Spreads.pdf, the reading edition with the back cover moved to the front so a two-page view pairs 2|3, 4|5 like the bound book.

VersionBuiltSizeWhat changed
v1413 Oct 202617.5 MBRetail Congress MENA 2026 photography and the MECSR Verified seal (341 listing cards, 7 Must-Visit pages). Seal legend on p78, photo credits on p382. Current.
v1312 Oct 202613.2 MBEvery QR code taken out of print: listing cards, country openers, the cover, the LISTING PENDING placeholders and every scan instruction. Pages 5, 78 and 381 rewritten.
v1210 Oct 202619.0 MBRebuilt from v10 page by page because the original generators did not survive. Every two-page item opens on a left-hand page; folios restamped to match the original type. Still has QR codes.

Why the QR codes went. Brilliant Directories builds a listing's web address from its name, so renaming a listing changes the address and breaks any printed code. If codes return in a later edition they need addresses that never change, for example a short link per listing ID that MECSR redirects itself.

Inside v14

Fourteen views from the reading edition. Stand-in photographs are captioned as stand-ins in the book itself.

What v14 added

  • Awards page (p66): the 2026 winners on stage, with a strip of three award moments.
  • House ads (pp 67–69): Retail People Magazine cover at the congress, the LEVEL UP sign and congress scenes, and an audience shot for GVS.

  • Expert Views (38–54), leadership messages (6–8), title partner page (2): congress photos as captioned stand-ins. Portrait and headshot boxes stay empty so nobody is pictured under someone else's name.
  • The seal: one vector mark, navy with a gold hairline and gold tick, bottom-right of the photo on 341 listing cards (300 nine-up, 41 six-up) and beside the name on the seven Must-Visit pages. Explained on p78; photography credited on p382.
  • Checks passed: 384 pages, spreads in order, text changed only on the overlay pages, no QR text left, folios unchanged.

Photos are from MEHAR SERIES; the page-by-page photo map is photo_map.json.

How a version is built

  1. Pages that change are rendered as HTML (pages_front.py, pages_v14.py) and printed to PDF in Chromium at A4 or an exact size (render.js, render_size.js).
  2. The assembler splices them into the previous book (assemble_v12.py, assemble_v13.py, assemble_v14.py), restamps folios and writes the print and reading editions.
  3. Lossless clean-up: dedupe_pdf.py merges repeated fonts and images to keep each file under 20 MB.
  4. Tracker and dossier: update_tracker.py applies the sponsor matrix, pagination and intel; patch_dossier.py refreshes the page proofs, the plan snapshot and the PDF tab in index.html.
Guards that stop a bad build. The assembler refuses a book that is not exactly 384 pages, v13's refuses one in which any QR code or scan instruction survives, and the dossier patcher refuses a plan that does not add to 384 or starts a two-page item on an odd page.

The scripts are saved on OneDrive in _build. They expect the image assets and Chromium of a Claude cloud session, so a rebuild means starting a session and pointing it at that folder.

The live flat-plan page

  • Address: orient-alt.github.io/mecsr-directory-2027, from the repository orient-alt/mecsr-directory-2027.
  • The loop: edit the workbook, commit it, refresh the page. Status, owners, sponsors, notes and page ranges are live; page artwork changes only when the book is rebuilt.
  • The Directory PDF tab finds the newest _v<N>_Spreads.pdf in the repository by itself.
  • Only the repository edition of the tracker may be committed (sheets 07–09 removed). GitHub Pages is public on the free plan; to require an @mecsc.org or @mecsr.org sign-in, move hosting to Cloudflare Pages with Cloudflare Access, or Azure Static Web Apps with Entra ID (steps in the README).
  • A scheduled task, MECSR Directory 2027 — Monday flat-plan check, reads the repository workbook every Monday at 08:00 Dubai and writes a status note to _weekly. It never pushes to GitHub. Its last run, on 12 Oct, failed on a usage limit.

File 02 of 04 · Mobile and web apps

Mobile and web apps: three directions

Field Guide, Intelligence Desk and Living Edition, each as a phone screen and a desktop page, with the benchmark and accessibility research behind them.

What exists

Three directions for the digital MECSR Directory, each drawn as a working phone screen and a working desktop page: six interactive artboards on one design canvas. All three run on the same structured database that feeds the print book.

  • Canvas: MECSR Digital Directory — Design Options (a Design artifact on Orient's account; share it to give a colleague access).
  • Files: Main.dc.html (A phone), FieldGuideDesktop.dc.html, DeskPhone.dc.html, DeskDesktop.dc.html, EditionPhone.dc.html, EditionDesktop.dc.html and canvas.json.
  • Data: 48 sample centres as printed in the v13 sample book, with the intel corrections from tracker sheet 11; 30 of them carry photos and the MECSR Verified seal as a design sample.
  • Last changes: the seal was added on 13 Oct; on 14 Oct the Field Guide phone's scroll area was adjusted in the design editor.

The screenshots below were rendered from the published artboards on 15 Oct 2026 with substitute fonts and grey boxes where the canvas photos sit, so spacing differs slightly from the canvas.

A · Field Guide: A search-first directory for phones

What it is

Search box first, five-tab bottom bar (Explore, Map, Saved, Pipeline, Edition), filter chips, list with a map toggle, saved shortlists, English and Arabic with full right-to-left mirroring.

Serves best

Leasing agents, retailers' expansion teams and Retail Congress delegates.

Trade-off

Editorial and sponsor spreads take a back seat, so sponsors need strong built-in placements; needs constant data upkeep.

B · Intelligence Desk: A data workspace for members

What it is

Sortable table of centres with saved searches and CSV export, a pipeline of openings from the intel, a weekly changes feed, and the before-print QA list.

Serves best

Investors, developers and consultants.

Trade-off

The most expensive to build and keep accurate; probably members-only, which limits reach and search visibility.

C · Living Edition: The directory as a publication

What it is

A finite edition between printings: stories built from the intel with dated sources, coming-soon openings, country profiles and links into the print reading edition.

Serves best

Senior executives, sponsors and new readers arriving from search or social media.

Trade-off

The heaviest editorial workload, doubled by two languages; weaker as a working tool.

What the research recommends

  • Make a responsive web edition the main digital product, with one web page per mall and provider, built mobile-first. Keep the page-faithful PDF or flipbook only as the secondary print edition.
  • Build the mobile web version before any native app. App installs fall from 75% of shoppers for their most-used site to 39% for their fifth (Baymard).
  • Target WCAG 2.2 AA (ISO/IEC 40500:2025): 24×24 px minimum targets, reflow at 320 px, focus never hidden by sticky bars, a list alternative to every map.
  • Arabic: lang="ar" dir="rtl", logical CSS properties, <bdi> around Latin names and numbers, no letter-spacing on Arabic, one digit system chosen explicitly.
  • Sponsors: label showcases "Advertisement / إعلان" beside the company name; payment never changes tiers, format codes or neutral sort orders.
  • Verification badge: a tappable badge that says when the record was last confirmed, as Bayut's TruCheck and Property Finder's Verified do.

Sources for every point are in the two briefs below and in file 00, "Every search".

The research briefs (10 Oct 2026)

Two research agents wrote these briefs from 166 searches and 193 pages opened. They are reproduced in full with their links.

Digital benchmark brief · reference products, flipbook vs responsive, ten listing patterns, sponsor norms, three directions

MECSR Directory 2027: digital benchmark brief

Research as of 10 Oct 2026. The starting point is that MECS+R's 2019–2024 directories are published as Issuu flipbooks (profile). Issuu's dashboard shows which devices people read on and how much traffic came from QR codes (help). Pull the 2024 edition's device split before choosing a format. I found no published MECSR usage figures.

(a) Reference products, ranked

  1. MICHELIN Guide (web + app): the closest analogue, with curated, tiered listings across many countries plus editorial. - The rating is both a filter and an icon. Users filter by distinction, cuisine and opening days, and a map icon switches any results to a map. Keys are "the equivalent of a Michelin Star for hotels". So S1–S6 and the format codes should be main filters, with a visible legend (16 Oct 2024). - A free account gives Favourites and Visited lists, and app users can "create and share lists" (App Store). - Michelin says tourism-board fees "do not have any influence on the Inspectors' judgments", but the press still scrutinises these deals (WKRG, 18 Apr 2026). MECSR should publish how tiers are assigned.

  2. CoStar / LoopNet: how commercial property professionals already expect search to work. - Map, List and Analytics views all show the same results, and filters can be changed in any of them. Users can draw a polygon, radius or corridor, save favourites, save and reload searches, and export to Excel (help). - Users can name a saved search and get daily or weekly alerts (LoopNet help). - What to avoid: paid tiers buy search position, with Diamond getting "the highest search placement available" (LoopNet). Propmodo criticises the "minimal transparency" this creates (19 Aug 2024).

  3. Bayut / Property Finder: the English/Arabic listing conventions GCC users already know. - Verification badges that explain themselves. Bayut's TruCheck badge (2019) can be tapped to show when the listing was last checked, it expires, and there is a "TruCheck First" option (Bayut, App Store). Property Finder has shown a "Verified" badge since 2015 (22 Jul 2024). - Market data sits beside listings: Bayut's Dubai Transactions with alerts, and Property Finder's transaction history and community comparison (App Store). - For MECSR: stamp each mall record "data verified [month/year]".

  4. Eater (maps + app): the model for linking editorial to listings. - Editors have built 10,000+ maps across 100+ cities, and these feed the app's listings. Each restaurant page shows why the editors chose it and every map it appears on. - The single presenting partner ("presented by Capital One Dining") pays for the product, not for any listing's position (SevenRooms, 10 Oct 2024). - For MECSR: each mall record should show "Featured in: KSA profile, Expert view X".

  5. Clutch: a B2B service-provider directory, the nearest match to the ~860 providers. - Sponsors appear above non-sponsors but "do not receive preferential treatment in Clutch rankings". Users can sort by Clutch Rank instead (help). - The ordering rules (sponsor tier first, then rank) are published (help). Clutch's docs don't say how sponsors are visually labelled.

  6. Malls.com + ICSC classification: the data model and the most useful filters. - Its fields match MECSR's: GLA, class, format, opening year, owner, manager, anchors, location. It filters by tenant brand, including the reverse ("malls without brand X"), and by GLA threshold, with CSV export. It covers 7,900+ centres in 50+ countries (Malls.com). - ICSC defines each format by GLA, anchor count and trade area; for example, Super-Regional is 800,000+ sq ft with 3+ anchors (ICSC, Jan 2017). MECSR should publish the thresholds for each S-tier and format code the same way.

  7. Crunchbase: a pattern for owner, manager, provider and member profiles. - A short About and Highlights summary sits at the top, with detail in tabs and a "Recent News & Activity" section. Save adds a company to custom lists and sends updates (updated 12 Nov 2025).

  8. MIPIM / EXPO REAL directories: event directories for the same investor and developer audience. - MIPIM lets users search by name, role, company, country and interests, add people to "My Network", and download favourites as a PDF (MIPIM). - EXPO REAL offers favourite companies and sessions, hall plans and matchmaking (EXPO REAL).

  9. The Economist app: reading a fixed edition on a phone. - Features include the edition ahead of print, a quick-scan "World in Brief", narrated articles with an audio queue, bookmarks, adjustable text size and dark mode (App Store).

  10. Apple News Format: how to design so content reflows.

    • Layouts are built on a column grid that automatically shrinks, from 10 columns on iPad Pro to 3 on an iPhone in portrait (Apple).
    • Contrast the PDF magazine pages many titles used when Apple News+ launched in 2019: "The PDF-style delivery completely sucks on a small iPhone screen" (Gizmodo, 12 Apr 2019).

  11. Shorthand / Readymag: tools for building features and sponsor showcases.

    • Shorthand says its pages are "fully responsive" and that Retail Week moved to it from print and PDF. That is the vendor's own claim (Shorthand).
    • Readymag first stacks a page into a single column automatically (one designer puts this at about 80% of the work), then designers adjust each screen size by hand (21 May 2026).

I also reviewed Wallpaper* (app from 2012), Time Out (last notable app update 2016) and Bloomberg. Their guide products are thin or dated, so I didn't rank them. Monocle feeds into section (d).

(b) Flipbook vs responsive: verdict

Make a responsive web edition, with one web page per mall and provider, the main digital product, built as a mobile-friendly web app. Keep a page-faithful flipbook or PDF only as a secondary "print edition" for the archive, downloads and sponsors' designed spreads.

  • Usability (NN/g, 9 Aug 2020). PDFs force mobile users to "pinch, zoom, squint, and scroll around out of context." Their advice: "Do not use PDFs to present digital content that could and should otherwise be a web page" (NN/g).
  • UK government digital service (16 Jul 2018). PDFs don't adapt to screen size and are harder to find, update and measure. Publish PDFs alongside HTML, not instead of it (GDS).
  • Accessibility standard (WCAG 2.2, criterion 1.4.10 Reflow, level AA). Content must work at 320 CSS px wide without scrolling both across and down. W3C accepts that print-sized layouts often "cannot simply reflow", but expects "an alternative presentation that does meet the requirements" (W3C).
  • Flipbook vendors admit accessibility is an add-on.
  • Flipsnack: it "does not make flipbook content accessible on its own" (help).
  • Fluidbook: text inside images is "invisible to screen readers" unless OCR is applied (page).
  • iPaper: the plain PDF "may still be the preferred option in some cases" (help).
  • Research and industry direction.
  • Page-turn copies of print "do not stand up to print" (Schijns & Smit, 2010, paper).
  • Readers remembered slightly less from digital replicas than from print (Neijens & Voorveld, 2018, paper).
  • PressReader is turning its replica product into a mobile news app (7 May 2026).
  • Issuu itself added mobile "Stories" cut out of PDF pages (29 May 2019).
  • The phone isn't the problem; the format is. People understood easy text as well on phones as on desktop, but hard text took longer. Dense B2B pages should be tested (NN/g, 11 Dec 2016).
  • Search visibility. Google does index text in PDFs (Google). But QR codes, sharing and search all need one stable web address per record.
  • Missing evidence. I found no independent study comparing engagement with flipbooks and responsive editions. Vendor uplift claims, such as 3D Issue's "two-fold increase", give no source.

(c) Ten listing patterns for mobile and web

  1. Search-first home with grouped suggestions. One box covers malls, cities, brands, companies and people. Show 4–8 suggestions on mobile, and style category suggestions (e.g. "Riyadh — in Malls") differently from plain ones (Baymard, 2 Aug 2022; NN/g, 20 May 2018).
  2. A visible bottom navigation bar with 3–5 sections. Google's Material Design recommends 3–5 sections of equal importance on phones (Material). Apple says tab bars are for navigation, not actions (Apple). Hiding navigation behind a menu cut how much content users found by more than 20% (NN/g, 26 Jun 2016).
  3. Filters. - Put 2–3 key filters (Country, Format, Tier) as buttons at the top of the list; 61% of sites don't do this (Baymard, 21 Nov 2023). - Keep the Filter & Sort button stuck on screen. Open filters in a bottom sheet with an Apply button that shows the result count, and make tap targets at least 44 pt (Baymard, 17 Apr 2026). - On mobile, apply filters together with one button rather than refreshing after each tap (NN/g, 7 Feb 2016). - Show active filters as removable tags (Baymard).
  4. List first on phones with a map toggle; list and map side by side on desktop (NN/g, 19 Jan 2014). Baymard found 65% of users on list-first sites never used the map, while 95% used Hilton's side-by-side view (8 Feb 2022).
  5. Uniform cards. Put the same fields in the same places on every card: name, city, GLA, opening year, tier icon, format and photo. Use no more than 2–3 badge types. 64% of sites show fields inconsistently (Baymard, 22 Aug 2023; NN/g).
  6. Compare. Allow 2 items on phones and up to 5 on desktop, with an "only show differences" option, grouped rows and headers that stay visible while scrolling (NN/g, 9 Feb 2024; Baymard).
  7. Easy saving. One tap to save, no forced login, named lists, and PDF or CSV export (NN/g, 4 Nov 2018).
  8. Direct links and QR codes. Each print QR code should open that exact record, not the homepage, with a short web address printed beside it. Make codes at least 2 × 2 cm and redirect old ones (NN/g, 9 Feb 2024). Use the phone's own share menu through the Web Share API (W3C, 30 May 2023).
  9. Memory and speed. - The Back button must bring back the user's filters, open panels and scroll position; 59% of sites break at least one of these (Baymard, 20 Jul 2020). - Use grey placeholder layouts only for full-page loads of 2–10 seconds (NN/g, 4 Jun 2023). - Store the edition and saved lists for offline use, and tell users when they're offline (web.dev).
  10. Proper English/Arabic mirroring. In Arabic, flip the layout, navigation and arrow icons. Don't flip numbers, charts or media controls, and keep Latin-script names left-to-right (Material). The most important spot on a card moves from top-left to top-right.

Build the mobile web version before any native app. Among US online shoppers, app installs fall from 75% for their most-used site to 39% for their fifth (Baymard, 15 Jun 2021).

(d) Sponsor presentation norms

  • Wording.
  • US regulator FTC (Dec 2015): "Ad", "Advertisement", "Paid Advertisement" and "Sponsored Advertising Content" are fine. "Promoted", "Presented by X" and "Brought to you by X" are ambiguous (summary).
  • UK advertising regulator ASA/CAP (23 Mar 2023): "Advertisement feature" and "Ad" are fine; it advises against "Sponsored" (ASA).
  • UAE National Media Council guide (undated): ads must be "clearly identified" and "distinct and independent from other editorial", and any financial relationship disclosed (NMC).
  • For MECSR: label showcases "Advertisement / إعلان" and promoted rows "Paid placement". Keep "Featured" for editorial picks. That last point is my inference; no regulator rules on the word.
  • Where the label goes.
  • Put it next to the company name, on a contrasting background, and keep it attached when the item is shared (FTC).
  • In a Danish regulator experiment, labels placed beside the listing name raised awareness of paid results from 25% to 65–71%. An icon on its own was understood by only 9% (Danish Competition and Consumer Authority, Apr 2022).
  • In one study, only 7% of readers recognised a native ad as advertising. The words "advertising" or "sponsored" were recognised seven times more often than "presented by". Labels in the middle of the page were looked at by 90% of readers, against 40% for labels at the top (Wojdynski & Evans, 2015). So repeat the label inside long showcases.
  • Paying must not change rankings. The EU's Omnibus Directive (2019/2161) requires disclosure whenever payment lifts a result's ranking. Follow Clutch's approach, not LoopNet's. Sponsorship should never affect S-tiers, format codes or neutral sort orders (GLA, A–Z, opening year).
  • Native in style, but clearly separate.
  • The New York Times "Paid Post" combines the advertiser's logo with a different typeface and a coloured bar (Poynter, 19 Dec 2013). It later dropped its heavy border (Aug 2014).
  • Monocle publishes co-branded "Monocle x World of Hyatt" city guides and keeps a separate "Partnered content" section (Monocle).
  • Dezeen Showroom is a separate paid section for product launches with its own index (Oct 2020).
  • Banner blindness. People skip anything that looks like an ad, and ads make the content next to them get ignored too (NN/g, 22 Apr 2018). Keep sponsor units away from the data, and make showcases genuinely useful (portfolio, pipeline, contacts).

(e) Three design directions

  1. Field Guide: a search-first mobile web app. - Borrows from: MICHELIN, Bayut/Property Finder, Eater, MIPIM/EXPO REAL. - What it is: search home, bottom navigation, list first with a map toggle, tier icons as filters, side-by-side compare of two, shortlists exported as PDF, a QR code to every record, and offline use at events. - Serves best: leasing agents, retailers' expansion teams and Retail Congress attendees. - Trade-off: editorial content and sponsor spreads take a back seat, so sponsors need strong built-in placements. It also needs constant data upkeep.
  2. Intelligence Desk: a data-heavy web workspace. - Borrows from: CoStar/LoopNet, Crunchbase, Malls.com, Clutch. - What it is: a desktop map beside a sortable table, "with brand X" and "without brand X" filters, draw-on-map search, saved searches with alerts for new openings, compare up to four, CSV export, charts (GLA by country, openings pipeline by year), and company profiles. - Serves best: investors, developers and consultants. - Trade-off: the most expensive to build and keep accurate, and weaker on phones. It would probably be members-only, which limits reach and search visibility, and it creates pressure to sell ranking.
  3. Living Edition: a responsive magazine-style edition linked to the listings. - Borrows from: The Economist, Eater, Apple News Format, NYT/Monocle, Shorthand/Readymag. - What it is: a finite English/Arabic edition with a contents page, expert views with audio, country profiles with maps and lists of top centres, and designed sponsor showcases labelled "Advertisement". Stories and records link to each other, and a print-replica PDF is available. - Serves best: senior executives, sponsors, and new readers arriving from search or social media. - Trade-off: the heaviest editorial workload each year, doubled by two languages. It's weaker as a working tool, and too many showcases would make it feel like a catalogue.

All three can run on one structured database that feeds print, web and QR codes. The real choice is which audience the front page is built for.

Accessibility and front-end standards brief · WCAG 2.2 AA, EU, UAE and Saudi rules, Arabic and RTL, performance, maps, PDF/UA

MECSR Directory 2027: accessibility and front-end standards brief (sources checked 10 Oct 2026, about 1,530 words)

Target: WCAG 2.2 Level AA across the web, the PWA and the HTML edition. - WCAG 2.2 has also been the ISO standard ISO/IEC 40500:2025 since 21 Oct 2025 (W3C). - 4.1.1 Parsing was removed in 2.2 (W3C). Full spec. - It goes beyond every regional baseline in §2.

1. WCAG 2.2 AA: the criteria this product is most likely to fail

  • 1.4.3 Contrast: text ≥4.5:1. Large text ≥3:1, where large means ≥18pt (≈24 CSS px) or ≥14pt bold (≈18.5px). Text over listing photos needs a scrim. Logos are exempt. W3C
  • 1.4.11 Non-text contrast: ≥3:1 for the edges and states of controls (filter chips, checkboxes, inputs), focus indicators, map pins and chart lines. W3C
  • 1.4.10 Reflow: no scrolling in two directions at 320 CSS px wide (the same as 1280px at 400% zoom). Maps and data tables are exempt; the filters, headings and pagination around them are not. Put each table in its own scroll container. W3C
  • 1.4.12 Text spacing: nothing clips when users set line-height 1.5×, paragraph spacing 2×, letter-spacing 0.12× and word-spacing 0.16× the font size. A script is exempt from properties it doesn't use (e.g. Arabic letter-spacing). No fixed-height cards. W3C
  • 1.4.13 Content on hover/focus: map-pin tooltips can be dismissed with Esc, can be hovered, and stay visible. W3C
  • 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide: auto-advancing sponsor carousels that run longer than 5 s need a visible pause control. W3C, tutorial
  • 2.4.11 Focus not obscured: the focused element is never entirely hidden by a sticky header, bottom nav, cookie bar or chat widget. Use scroll-padding. W3C
  • 2.5.7 Dragging: every drag action needs a single-tap/click alternative. W3C's own examples match this product: map arrow buttons, sliders you can tap anywhere on the track, carousel buttons. W3C
  • 2.5.8 Target size: at least 24×24 CSS px. Smaller targets pass if a 24px circle centred on each one touches no other target or circle.
  • Exceptions: inline links, an equivalent larger control, browser-default controls, and "essential" presentation. W3C gives dense map pins as an example of "essential".
  • The stricter AAA level (2.5.5) is 44×44. W3C
  • 3.1.1/3.1.2 Language: set lang="ar" or lang="en" on each page. Mark English passages inside Arabic pages; proper names are exempt. Label the language switcher in its own language. W3C
  • 3.2.6 Consistent help (A): contact details, contact form, FAQ and chatbot appear in the same relative order on every page. W3C
  • 3.3.7 Redundant entry (A): listing-update and enquiry flows fill in, or offer to reuse, anything the user already entered. W3C
  • 3.3.8 Accessible authentication: if centre managers log in, allow pasting and password managers. No puzzle CAPTCHA without an alternative. W3C
  • 4.1.2 Name/role/value: use native button, input and select. Filter chips must expose their checked/pressed state; accordions expose aria-expanded. W3C
  • 4.1.3 Status messages: announce results like "214 centres match" with role="status", without moving focus. W3C
  • Modals: role="dialog", aria-modal="true" and a label. Tab cycles inside the dialog, Esc closes it, and focus goes back to the button that opened it. APG
  • Zoom: never set user-scalable=no. MDN

2. Legal and regulatory

  • EU: European Accessibility Act (Directive 2019/882) (Text, Art. 4)
  • It applies to listed services "provided to consumers after 28 June 2025", including e-commerce services and e-books (Art. 2(2)).
  • A "service provider" includes anyone who "makes offers to provide such a service to consumers in the Union" (Art. 3(4)). Being based outside the EU is no exemption.
  • A "consumer" acts "outside his trade, business, craft or profession" (Art. 3(22)).
  • Microenterprises (fewer than 10 staff and ≤€2m turnover or balance sheet) are exempt for services (Art. 4(5)).
  • My reading, not legal advice: a free B2B trade directory is probably out of scope. Selling editions or subscriptions to EU individuals could bring it into scope. Get a lawyer to confirm.
  • EN 301 549 V4.1.1, the EU technical standard used with the EAA, was published 2 Sep 2026 and moves to WCAG 2.2 A/AA. Meeting it only counts as presumed compliance once it is cited in the EU's Official Journal; Deque expects that around 30 Nov 2026. DWT, Deque
  • UAE: National Digital Accessibility Policy (TDRA, 18 Mar 2024) (Policy, portal, UAE Design System)
  • Annex 1: "All public service sites must comply with Level AA of the WCAG 2.1". This binds federal entities.
  • Its objectives name private companies "involved in creating and publishing different kinds of digital content". That plausibly covers MECSR if it is UAE-based.
  • Private entities only have to "exert the best efforts in compliance".
  • Saudi Arabia: Digital Government Authority (DGA) (DGA)
  • The "Guideline For Web Accessibility of Digital Channels Content…" (DGA-1-2-4-203 v2.0, dated 12/05/2024) covers WCAG 2.2.
  • Its audience includes the private sector "that develop or operate digital government-related activities".
  • The page states no conformance level and doesn't say whether it is binding.
  • Not confirmed from official sources: a vendor's claims that the DGA enforces WCAG 2.1 AA with an April 2026 deadline.
  • Net: I found no confirmed hard mandate on a private B2B directory in the UAE or Saudi Arabia (the UAE asks for best efforts). WCAG 2.2 AA goes beyond every cited baseline.

3. Arabic and RTL

  • Use <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">. Never set the base direction in CSS. Put dir="auto" (plus dirname) on search and other user-entered fields. W3C i18n
  • Use logical CSS only: margin-inline-start, padding-inline, inset-inline, text-align:start. MDN
  • Wrap every inserted Latin brand or mall name, URL, email and phone number in <bdi> or an element with dir (unicode-bidi:isolate). Otherwise numbers "stick" to the Arabic text next to them. W3C
  • Mirror: back/next chevrons, list and text-flow icons, steppers, sliders, linear progress bars. Don't mirror: media controls and scrubbers, clocks, checkmarks, logos, slashes, photos, digits and phone numbers. Apple, Wikimedia Codex
  • Digits: decide once and set explicitly. alreq, MDN
  • alreq: European digits (0–9) are used in the Maghreb, Arabic-Indic digits (٠–٩) in the Eastern Arab countries such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt. Apple: Arabic text "might use either".
  • Locale defaults differ within the GCC. In my test on Node 22 (ICU 77.1/CLDR 47), ar and ar-AE gave 0–9, while ar-SA/QA/KW/BH/OM/EG gave ٠–٩.
  • Force one system with ar-u-nu-latn or ar-u-nu-arab. Runs of digits always read left to right.
  • No letter-spacing on Arabic text: it breaks the joins between letters. A CSS Text 3 browser test asserts it "must not be applied to Arabic text". Reset it with :lang(ar){letter-spacing:0}. spec
  • Vertical room: Arabic ascenders and descenders "extend much further than those of the Latin script" (alreq §7.4). Material classes Arabic as a "tall" script (Flutter/Material). Apple suggests about 2pt larger for Arabic set beside all-caps Latin. No standard prescribes a line-height, so test with real copy.
  • Fonts (all SIL Open Font License 1.1):
  • IBM Plex Sans Arabic: static weights 100–700; pairs with IBM Plex Sans. (link)
  • Noto Sans Arabic: variable weight 100–900 plus a width axis; pairs with Noto Sans. (link)
  • Noto Kufi Arabic: variable 100–900; for headings. (link)
  • Noto Naskh Arabic: 400–700; for long-form articles. (link)
  • Cairo: Arabic and Latin, variable 200–1000. (link)
  • Tajawal: Arabic and Latin, static 200–900. (link)
  • Readex Pro: Arabic and Latin, a "world-script expansion of Lexend", variable 160–700. (link)
  • Reference: W3C Arabic & Persian Layout Requirements (alreq), Group Draft Note, 2 Oct 2025. alreq

4. Performance and mobile

  • Core Web Vitals, measured at the 75th percentile, mobile and desktop separately (vitals):
  • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) ≤2.5 s; poor above 4 s. LCP
  • INP (Interaction to Next Paint) ≤200 ms; poor above 500 ms. It replaced FID on 12 Mar 2024. INP
  • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) ≤0.1; poor above 0.25. CLS
  • Images:
  • srcset with width descriptors plus sizes; <picture> ordered AVIF, then WebP, then JPEG. (web.dev)
  • width/height or aspect-ratio on every image. (web.dev)
  • loading="lazy" only below the fold. Never lazy-load the main hero image; give it fetchpriority="high" and reference it directly in the HTML. (web.dev)
  • Fonts: (web.dev)
  • WOFF2 only. Use font-display: swap, or optional for the least layout shift.
  • Split Arabic and Latin with unicode-range so English pages never download Arabic glyphs. Note that preload ignores unicode-range.
  • Use size-adjust on fallback fonts.
  • Subset with a tool that preserves Arabic shaping: fontTools keeps "all features required for script shaping" by default. (fontTools)
  • PWA:
  • Chrome's install criteria: HTTPS, and a manifest with name/short_name, 192px and 512px icons, start_url, and display set to standalone, minimal-ui, fullscreen or window-controls-overlay. (Chrome criteria)
  • Add a maskable icon, and give each language edition its own manifest using lang/dir. (manifest)
  • web.dev's Chrome criteria page (updated Sep 2024) no longer lists a service worker, but you need one for an offline fallback page. (offline)
  • Safe areas: viewport-fit=cover plus env(safe-area-inset-*) with fallback values on sticky footers and the bottom nav. MDN
  • Motion and dark mode: under prefers-reduced-motion, stop autoplay, parallax and animated map fly-to (MDN). If you offer dark mode via prefers-color-scheme, re-test 1.4.3 and 1.4.11 in both themes (MDN).
  • Touch targets: the WCAG floor is 24px, but design to the platform sizes:
  • Apple: "at least 44 points x 44 points" (Apple).
  • Android/Material: 48×48dp (about 9mm), at least 8dp apart (Google).

5. Maps and tables

  • The map is never the only way in: provide a list view with the same results and filters, and addresses as text (WCAG 1.1.1). BOIA
  • Pins work by keyboard and each has a unique name:
  • Google Advanced Markers: set gmpClickable and title. Tab reaches the first marker, arrow keys move between markers, Enter/Space opens one, and focus returns to the marker when its info window closes. (Google)
  • Leaflet markers work by keyboard by default; give each a unique alt or title. (Leaflet)
  • Zoom and pan buttons (2.5.7); pins at 3:1 contrast (1.4.11); cluster badges show their count as text.
  • Sortable tables: APG
  • Use <table>, <caption> and <th scope>.
  • Each sort control is a <button> inside its <th>.
  • aria-sort goes only on the column currently sorted, and the arrow icons are aria-hidden.

6. Downloadable PDF edition

  • Standard: conform to PDF/UA-1 (ISO 14289-1, 2012; 2nd edition 2014) or PDF/UA-2 (ISO 14289-2:2024, based on PDF 2.0, published 13 Mar 2024). PDF Association, ISO
  • Tagging basics, as checked by the Matterhorn Protocol (the PDF/UA test list) (list):
  • Everything is either tagged as content or marked as a decorative artifact (checkpoint 01).
  • Title set in the metadata, with DisplayDocTitle true (06/07).
  • Every glyph maps to Unicode (10-001), which is critical for shaped Arabic text.
  • Document /Lang plus a language on each foreign-language passage (11; PDF16).
  • Alt text on figures (13-004).
  • Headings H1–H6 with no skipped levels (14).
  • Table header cells tagged TH with Scope (15).
  • Arabic export from InDesign can produce left-to-right tag order. Thread the stories, map paragraph styles to tags, and check the tag order. Adobe forum
  • Validate with PAC (free, Windows only) (VT) and veraPDF (open source, PDF/UA-1 and -2) (Flathub).
  • A flipbook is an optional extra, never the main format. The evidence:
  • The flipbook vendor 3D Issue says flipbooks are "image-based, meaning that text to speech solutions will not work" (3D Issue).
  • The University of South Wales says Issuu can "strip away our accessible PDF features" (USW).
  • Northern Michigan University requires a tested accessible PDF alongside every flipbook (NMU).
  • The UK Government Digital Service: "The default should be to create all content in HTML" (GDS).
  • My own reading of WCAG: pages rendered as images also fail 1.4.5 Images of Text and can't reflow (1.4.10).
  • So the order is: HTML articles first, then the tagged PDF as a download, then the flipbook as an extra.

Could not confirm: - Saudi Arabia: the required conformance level and whether the DGA guideline is binding. - Any numeric Arabic line-height in a standard. - Whether the EAA applies to MECSR's actual sales model; that needs a lawyer.

File 03 of 04 · Sourcing and verification plan

Sourcing and verification plan

Where the directory's data comes from, and how every landlord is asked to confirm their record before the 2027 edition goes to print.

The plan in one view

MECSR researches each record and the landlord only confirms it. All 1,150 Brilliant listings are asked "Is this still correct?" between 3 Nov 2026 and 15 Apr 2027, so the 2027 edition prints MECSR Verified only on records an operator has checked.

1,150listings in scope (1,078 malls, 51 brands, 21 service providers)
457messages to 410 owner accounts, one per contact per wave
0landlord-confirmed today
450contacts to check before sending
15 Apr 2027confirmations close, 3 weeks before the data freeze
35%target for all listings; 60% for waves 1–2

The working copy is the Claude Doc MECSR Verified 2027 — Landlord Confirmation Campaign. This file mirrors it as of 15 Oct 2026, adds the sourcing side and lists the files. A PDF of the doc, exported on 16 Oct 2026, is in Offline copies for anyone the link cannot reach.

Ian's model (12 Oct 2026)

From MECSR Directory Getting Landlords to Confirm Their Data.pdf. Members do not update profiles because there is nothing in it for them, and reminder emails will not change that.

Part 1 · Collect it ourselves

  • Listed developers' disclosures: Tadawul, DFM and ADX annual reports and investor presentations.
  • Developer and project announcements; government sources (planning approvals, tenders, giga-projects); trade press and RPM.
  • Leasing signals: a GM or leasing-team job advert means an opening within 12–18 months.
  • A weekly AI monitoring task pulls mall names, GLA, status and dates, and flags changes.
  • Each landlord then gets a pre-filled profile with one question, "Is this still correct?": 30 seconds instead of 30 minutes for a blank form.

Make it effortless

  • Email or WhatsApp with confirm and edit links, no login.
  • Ask 5–8 fields, not 50.
  • Send to marketing and leasing managers, not CEOs; GVS alumni sit in these teams.
  • One annual confirmation window with a deadline tied to publication.

Who first

  1. Upcoming and under-construction projects.
  2. The top 100 operating assets by GLA.
  3. Smaller community centres later.

Recommendation: flip to "we've researched you, please confirm" and make a confirmed profile a condition of entering the MECSR Awards. Next step: brief the build of the AI monitoring pipeline that drafts the pre-filled profiles.

MECSR source policy, as the intel tasks apply it

  • A · Primary and official: company investor-relations pages, stock-exchange filings, ministries, regulators and national news agencies. Highest confidence.
  • B · Established regional and international media: outlets with named journalists, dates and a corrections process.
  • C · Discovery only: aggregators, property portals, LinkedIn posts and blogs, used to find leads that are then verified through A or B, never cited.
  • D · Do not use: anonymous or unverifiable posts, Wikipedia as a primary source, AI summaries without cited originals, publishers that cannot be identified.
  • Every item carries its publication date; MECSR's own website is never used to verify a record.

Scheduled research

  • MECSR Intel daily: weekdays at about 08:00 Dubai, following the skill file in mecsr-intel-daily on the office PC. Enabled since 14 Oct 2026; it is the natural home for Ian's weekly monitoring pass.
  • MECSR Directory 2027 — Monday flat-plan check: Mondays 08:00 Dubai, reads the repository tracker and writes a status note. Enabled.
  • Mecsr weekly intel report and Weekly gcc cx news digest: switched off on 14 Oct 2026.

Where we start

No listing is landlord-confirmed for 2027. The export labels 666 listings "Verified by MECSR (2026)", but 654 of them carry the same update stamp, 26 Jun 2026 at 09:51:06: one system edit, not 654 landlord checks.

  • Records are mostly complete, which is what makes pre-filling work: for the malls, GLA 93%, shop counts 89%, opening year 96%, managing company 97%; developer is the weak field at 52%.
  • Contacts are the gap. About 700 listings sit on an account that matches the landlord. The other 450 need the contact checked first: 201 uploaded by consultants or a publisher, 102 on claim accounts with no company named, 80 on MECSR staff accounts and 67 on accounts that do not match the listing. 55 contacts are CEO-level and should be re-routed to marketing or leasing.
  • The first Confirmation Plan sheet in the export targets only the 459 stale listings and badges the 666 as verified. Its badge rule (cell B8) needs changing to match.

How confirmation works

  1. Research and pre-fill each record from Ian's sources; changes are marked as MECSR research.
  2. Send one question: the listings printed back under "Is this still correct?" with Yes, it's correct and Something's changed. A contact with several listings gets one message covering all of them.
  3. Confirm without a login: Yes opens a short form with the listing ID filled in; the contact adds name, role and work email and presses Submit. Something's changed opens the same form with the fields to correct. A plain email reply also counts.
  4. Update Brilliant: the verification desk applies edits, records the confirmed date and switches on the MECSR Verified 2027 seal.
  5. Send a receipt with the seal and the date; reminders for that listing stop.

A tracked click alone cannot count as a confirmation, because corporate mail scanners open links automatically. The eight fields asked: centre name; city and country; status; opening year or expected opening; retail GLA in sqm (leasable, not built-up); number of shops; owner and developer; managing company and leasing contact.

eSputnik notes. Text fields are written ${verify.name}; in a button or link the field is written %VERIFY.LISTING_ID%, and the dollar form in a link is not substituted in real campaigns (Dynamic Links in Email, Personalization by Merge Tags). Text inputs hold 1,000 characters and text areas 5,000, and may not contain % ^ * | ~ { (Contact Fields). Microsoft Forms can pre-fill answers from a link (Neowin).

The Awards, Congress and renewal levers are commercial, so account managers use them in their own conversations; the bulk emails stay administrative.

Timeline

No sends over the year-end break or during Ramadan. Inside each wave: E1 on a Tuesday, E2 a week later, the nudge two days after that, E3 at two weeks and E4 at three; waves 3b–c skip E4 and the March last call covers them.

Team, tools and tracking

  • Campaign lead: dates, sends, the Monday numbers. Research desk: checks the 450 doubtful contacts and pre-fills records. Verification desk: replies, Brilliant updates, the seal and receipts within two working days. Account managers: heads-up, calls for waves 1–2, commercial levers.
  • Tools: eSputnik from an authenticated domain; Microsoft Forms with pre-filled answers saving to Excel on OneDrive; two new Brilliant fields, Verified 2027 and Confirmed on; one shared reply inbox.
  • Status codes: To check · Ready · Sent · Confirmed · Confirmed with edits · Seal on · Wrong contact · Bounced · Opted out · Remove requested.
Monday numberTargetWarning sign

Replies to E1—Under 3%: the subject or the sender is wrong
Bounces—Over 8%: stop the wave and clean the list
Opt-outs—Over 1%: the emails read as marketing
Working days from reply to seal2A backlog of more than 50

Rules

  • Personal data stays private. Contact names, emails and phone numbers live only in the OneDrive campaign workbook and eSputnik (UAE and Saudi PDPL).
  • Say why, make it easy to stop. Each message names the listing and the reason, with a one-click opt-out honoured within one working day.
  • Nothing that looks like phishing. No attachments, passwords or logins; links only to MECSR's domain or the form; a named sender on an authenticated domain.
  • Verified cannot be bought. Sponsors buy visibility, never data placement, rankings or MECSR Verified status (book pp. 2 and 380).
  • Only the landlord confirms, on a company address; a webmail reply gets a call-back check.
  • Keep the evidence: who, when, which fields changed, which form or email.
  • Research is labelled as research until the landlord confirms it; no listing is removed for not answering.

  • The seal needs a landlord's confirmation and the 26 June bulk edit does not count; change cell B8 of the export's Confirmation Plan sheet.
  • Whether a confirmed listing is required to enter the MECSR Awards 2027.
  • Who signs the emails, who leads, who staffs the two desks.
  • The form tool (Microsoft Forms with pre-filled answers by default) and the reply inbox.

  • Build the form, paste its pre-filled link into Setup, put the two links and eSputnik's unsubscribe link into the templates; test-send to Outlook, Gmail and a phone.
  • Add the Brilliant fields, ready to show the seal from 30 Nov.
  • Check the 66 doubtful contacts in waves 1–2 and pre-fill those 178 records.
  • Brief the AI monitoring task so it feeds wave 3; set the GCC supply report date.

Claude memory handoff

The context, rules, decisions and file map another Claude account needs to pick up the MECSR Directory 2027 work without starting over.

How to hand this to another Claude account

  1. Keep the five files together in one folder; file 00 links to the rest. Or send the single file MECSR_Session_Record_All_in_One.html, which holds all five as tabs. Both are in MECSR Session Record.
  2. In the colleague's Claude, start a Project (or a new chat), upload this file and whichever of files 01–03 matter, then paste the text below as the first message or into the Project instructions. If memory is switched on in that account, ask Claude to remember it.
  3. Ask Orient to share what the colleague needs on claude.ai: this record's online page, the campaign doc, the design canvas and the dossier. Artifact links do not open for anyone they are not shared with. If Share cannot reach the colleague's account, use the files: Offline copies holds the campaign doc as a PDF and the canvas source, and the dossier is MECSR_2027_Directory_Dossier.html.
  4. Give the colleague the OneDrive folder Directory 2026 and, if they work in Cowork on their own computer, connect that folder there.
  5. Scheduled tasks belong to Orient's account and stay there. The colleague recreates any they need from the prompts in the internal edition.

The text to give Claude

About 900 words. Contains no personal contact data.

Things that went wrong before

  • OneDrive files that are only online can fail to open in the device shell with "Invalid argument"; staging the file into the cloud workspace works.
  • The photo drive RCM 2026 does not mount in the device shell; list and stage files from it with the file tools instead.
  • The browser upload tool rejects files over 10 MB, so the 13–18 MB book PDFs have to be dragged into GitHub by hand. Small files can be committed through the web page.
  • Do not try to work around GitHub's upload page by injecting elements into it; that was blocked and should not be retried.
  • GitHub Pages can serve a cached page after a push; add ?fresh=1 to the address to check.
  • A file that is open in Excel cannot be overwritten from the device; save results under a new name beside it.
  • The book build needs Chromium, PyMuPDF and the image assets of a cloud session; say which pages each version re-renders.
  • In eSputnik, merge fields inside button links must use the %LIST.FIELD% form; the ${list.field} form previews but is not substituted in real sends.
  • The design canvas runs each artboard with its own data and logic; photos are stored inside the canvas and must be re-added if the files are moved.
